name: Phenylketonuria

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: ACMG ACT Sheet and Confirmatory Algorithm for PKU

criteria.description: Elevated blood phenylalanine (>120 micromol/L or >2 mg/dL) on newborn screening
Confirmatory plasma amino acid analysis showing elevated phenylalanine with normal or low tyrosine
Pathogenic variants identified in PAH gene (biallelic)
Normal biopterin metabolism (to exclude BH4 deficiency)
Classification by severity: classic PKU (>1200 micromol/L), moderate (900-1200), mild (600-900), mild HPA (120-600)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Persistently elevated blood phenylalanine >120 micromol/L with normal biopterin cofactor metabolism, confirmed by plasma amino acid analysis
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Universal newborn screening detects PKU before symptoms develop. Without treatment, classic PKU leads to severe intellectual disability. BH4 cofactor deficiency must be excluded as it requires different treatment.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Elevated blood phenylalanine on newborn screening
pathognomonic.notes: Biochemical rather than clinical; detected before symptoms in screened populations
Due to phenylacetic acid in sweat and urine; only in untreated or poorly controlled patients

common.notes: Severe if untreated; IQ loss of 50+ points; prevented by early dietary treatment

common.symptomName: Fair skin, hair, and eyes (relative to family)
common.notes: Due to inhibition of melanin synthesis by excess phenylalanine
Infantile spasms or generalized seizures in untreated classic PKU
In untreated or poorly controlled patients

occasional.notes: Subtle cognitive effects may persist despite early treatment

rare.notes: Periventricular white matter changes; may be seen even in treated adults with poor dietary control

rare.symptomName: Maternal PKU syndrome (in offspring of untreated pregnant women with PKU)
rare.notes: Congenital heart defects, microcephaly, IUGR in offspring of poorly controlled maternal PKU
Reported in adult PKU patients; multifactorial etiology

laboratory: Elevated blood phenylalanine (>120 micromol/L; classic PKU >1200 micromol/L)
Normal biopterin cofactor studies (to exclude BH4 deficiency)
Elevated urinary phenylpyruvic acid, phenylacetic acid, phenyllactic acid (untreated)
imaging: MRI brain may show periventricular white matter T2 hyperintensities in poorly controlled patients
MRI findings reversible with improved metabolic control
genetic: Biallelic pathogenic variants in PAH gene (chromosome 12q23.2)
BH4 responsiveness correlates with specific PAH genotypes
other: Newborn screening by tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS)
BH4 loading test to assess cofactor responsiveness
Regular blood phenylalanine monitoring for dietary management

distinguishingFeatures: BH4 deficiency has abnormal biopterin metabolism studies
BH4 deficiency causes neurotransmitter deficiency (dopamine, serotonin)
Requires neurotransmitter replacement therapy in addition to dietary management
Different genetic etiology (GCH1, PTS, QDPR, PCBD genes)
MSUD has elevated branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine)
MSUD has sweet/maple syrup odor, not musty odor
Different amino acid profile on plasma analysis

redFlags: Untreated or late-diagnosed PKU with severe intellectual disability
Maternal PKU: uncontrolled phenylalanine during pregnancy causing fetal damage
Loss of dietary control in adolescents/adults leading to cognitive decline
Concurrent BH4 deficiency (requires different treatment approach)
Phenylalanine >600 micromol/L in treated patients (suboptimal control)
references: Vockley J, et al. Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency: diagnosis and management guideline. Genet Med. 2014;16(2):188-200.
van Wegberg AMJ, et al. The complete European guidelines on phenylketonuria: diagnosis and treatment. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2017;12(1):162.
Blau N, et al. Phenylketonuria. Lancet. 2010;376(9750):1417-27.
Camp KM, et al. Phenylketonuria Scientific Review Conference: State of the science and future research needs. Mol Genet Metab. 2014;112(2):87-122.
